title: The dancing peacock
hook: a peacock dances without modesty and loses his bride (Jataka 32)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a young man built a fortune starting with a dead mouse. Your line was from a dead mouse. Did you start something small? Today, someone who already has everything, and throws it away in a minute. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

Every bird in the mountains has gathered in one place. The king of the birds, a golden goose, has promised his daughter she may choose her own husband, and now she walks along the rows of feathered hopefuls. She stops in front of the peacock, with his jewel-colored neck and his patterned tail, and says: that one. In the Nacca Jataka, that should be the end. It's the beginning of his mistake.
screen: `ALL THE BIRDS GATHER.` → `SHE CHOOSES HER OWN.` → `SHE CHOOSES THE PEACOCK.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. In a time long ago, the tale says, the four-footed animals made the lion their king, the fish chose a great fish, and the birds chose the golden goose. His daughter asks one wish of her father: to pick her husband herself. He agrees, and calls the assembly. Second, the choice. She picks the peacock. The other birds go to him with the news. And he's so thrilled, so eager to show what he's got, that he says: she hasn't even seen my dancing yet. Third, the dance. Right there, in front of the king, the bride, and every bird in the mountains, the peacock spreads his feathers wide and dances. He's so busy showing off that he forgets himself completely and loses every bit of modesty, there in the middle of the crowd. Fourth, the cost. The golden goose is embarrassed for everyone. He speaks a verse: your voice is pleasant, your back is lovely, your neck has the color of a jewel, but for that dance I won't give you my daughter. He has no shame inside and no restraint outside, the king says. And he gives his daughter instead to a young goose, his own nephew. The peacock flies off, ashamed. Notice what the tale doesn't say. It doesn't say the peacock was ugly, or unworthy, or unloved. He'd already been chosen. Nothing more was needed from him. The win was finished, and the urge to prove it is what undid it. The Jataka tells it for a monk who forgot restraint in front of everyone.
screen: `A LION, A FISH, A GOLDEN GOOSE.` · `SHE PICKS THE PEACOCK.` · `HE DANCES IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.` · `GIVEN TO THE YOUNG GOOSE INSTEAD.` · then, large: `THE DANCE COST HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: skip one chance to show off. Bring to mind a place where you're tempted to. A meeting, a group chat, a dinner table, a post you're about to share. Notice the little lift in the chest, the urge to make sure everyone sees. Don't scold it. Just feel it rise, and feel it pass, the way a breath rises and passes. Whatever is already settled can stay settled. Rest in that, and let the dance stay undanced. The bell holds the time.
The dancing peacock. Already chosen, he shows off in front of everyone and loses the bride he'd already won. Today's word.
Your line: the dance cost him. Today, when you feel the urge to prove what's already settled, keep your feathers folded once. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the Nacca Jataka as a lesson in restraint and a sense of shame, hiri and ottappa in Pali.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fable about a vain bird.
what it means: the peacock had already won; showing off in front of everyone is what lost it.
what a scholar hears: the king's complaint is that he lacks shame inside and restraint outside; the Jataka tells it for a monk who lost restraint before the assembly.

notes: 'thirty-second tale' in the hook is the tale's number in the collection (Jataka 32); cut if the Keeper prefers no numbering.

Confirm details of Jataka 32: the first age, lion king of quadrupeds, a great fish king of fish, golden goose (hamsa) king of birds; the daughter's wish to choose her own husband; she chooses the peacock; he dances and exposes himself; the king's verse praising voice, back and beryl-colored neck, then refusing; daughter given to a young goose, the king's nephew.
Immodesty handled discreetly ('loses every bit of modesty'); confirm this is acceptable.
Frame story (a monk with many possessions who strips before the assembly) mentioned only as 'a monk who lost restraint'. Confirm.
howItsDone: hiri and ottappa (shame and moral dread) are described as guardians of conduct; confirm the phrasing.
